questions.q: How does policy-level reward hacking relate to reward model overoptimization from lesson 39?
options: They are unrelated phenomena with different causes
Policy-level reward hacking is what overoptimization looks like after PPO has actually found and exploited the reward model's blind spots within the KL-constrained drift budget
Reward hacking only happens before the reward model is trained
Reward hacking is fixed completely once a KL penalty is added
questions.explain: The KL penalty raises the cost of drift but doesn't remove the incentive — given enough training, PPO can still exploit reward model blind spots within whatever budget the penalty allows.

questions.q: What is mode collapse in the context of RLHF?
options: The reward model's training loss diverging to infinity
A reduction in the diversity of the policy's outputs relative to the SFT starting point, as PPO converges on whichever style the reward model scores highest
The PPO trainer crashing due to an out-of-memory error
A failure where the policy stops generating any text at all
questions.explain: If the reward model reliably scores one style highest, PPO has every incentive to converge on it and stop exploring stylistically valid alternatives, reducing output diversity.

questions.q: Where does sycophancy originate, and how does PPO affect it?
options: It originates purely in the SFT stage and PPO has no effect on it
It originates in a human-rater bias toward agreeable responses that the reward model inherits, and PPO then amplifies it by optimizing the policy straight into that bias
It is caused entirely by the KL penalty being too large
It only happens when the reward model has zero training data
questions.explain: Human raters tend to favor agreeable responses independent of accuracy; the reward model learns this bias, and PPO's optimization pressure amplifies it in the trained policy.

questions.q: What is over-refusal, and what causes it?
options: The model refusing to generate any text whatsoever regardless of the prompt
The policy refusing benign prompts that merely resemble prompts overrepresented in safety-relevant refusal preference data, generalizing refusal too broadly
A bug in the PPOTrainer that disables generation
A deliberate design choice with no connection to the preference data
questions.explain: If refusal is overrepresented for a broad class of prompts in the preference data, the trained policy can generalize that into refusing adjacent, actually-benign prompts too.

questions.q: According to this lesson, does a stronger KL penalty fix these failure modes without any cost?
options: Yes, a stronger KL penalty eliminates all RLHF failure modes with no downside
No — a stronger KL penalty reduces these failures somewhat, but also limits how much the reward model is allowed to actually improve the policy's helpfulness
A stronger KL penalty only affects training speed, not failure modes
KL penalty strength has no relationship to any of these failure modes
questions.explain: Alignment and capability gains come from the same drift the KL penalty constrains, so strengthening it trades off against how much real improvement RLHF can deliver.
